missing_details: To be fully stand-alone, the question should specify that the growth under discussion is word growth with respect to finite generating sets.
It should define the growth rate attached to a finite generating set S, e.g. via the word balls B_{G,S}(n) and the exponential growth rate omega(G,S) = lim_{n->infty} |B_{G,S}(n)|^(1/n).
It should define "uniformly exponential growth" as the condition inf_S omega(G,S) > 1, where S ranges over all finite generating sets of G.

It should make explicit that "of exponential growth but not of uniformly exponential growth" means: for at least one finite generating set S, omega(G,S) > 1, while inf_T omega(G,T) = 1 over all finite generating sets T.
It should define "just-infinite" as infinite with every nontrivial normal subgroup of finite index, and "hereditarily just-infinite" as every finite-index subgroup being just-infinite.

For maximal self-containment, it is helpful to say explicitly that the ambient objects are abstract finitely generated groups, not profinite or pro-p groups; elsewhere in the notebook, pro-p variants are flagged explicitly, for example in Problem 14.57. refined_question: Question 21.117. (a) Does there exist a finitely generated simple abstract group G such that G is of exponential growth but not of uniformly exponential growth; that is, if for a finite generating set S one writes B_{G,S}(n) for the radius-n word ball and omega(G,S) = lim_{n->infty} |B_{G,S}(n)|^(1/n), then omega(G,S) > 1 for some finite generating set S, but inf_T omega(G,T) = 1 when T ranges over all finite generating sets of G? (b) Does there exist a finitely generated hereditarily just-infinite abstract group G with the same growth property? Here, "just-infinite" means that G is infinite and every nontrivial normal subgroup of G has finite index, and "hereditarily just-infinite" means that every finite-index subgroup of G is just-infinite.
